summary: This informational document reclassifies seven Suite B related RFCs, 5759, 6239, 6318, 6379, 6380, 6403 and 6460, as Historic, and discusses why. Suite B refers to cryptographic algorithms of the US National Security Agency.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old rule books are put on the shelf marked 'old' because newer ones have replaced them.

questions: what happened to suite b rfcs
why were suite b documents made historic
when did nsa switch to cnsa suite
subtitle: Archive of superseded NSA Suite B cryptographic standards

tldr.problem: NSA's Suite B cryptographic standards and the RFCs describing their use in security protocols were published between 2007 and 2012, but NSA has transitioned to the newer CNSA Suite, leaving Suite B RFCs without active support.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reclassifies ten Suite B-related RFCs as Historic status: RFCs 4869, 5008, 5430, 5759, 6239, 6318, 6379, 6380, 6403, and 6460.
tldr.outcome: Suite B documents are now clearly marked as historical with no interoperability or security concerns for existing implementations that may continue to reference them.

today: RFC 8423 is Historic as of July 2018. The ten Suite B-related RFCs it covers are also Historic. CNSA Suite is now the recommended standard for new cryptographic deployments.

sections.title: Suite B and Its Replacement
sections.content:
Suite B was a set of cryptographic algorithms approved by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for use in security protocols. Between 2007 and 2012, the IETF published ten RFCs specifying how Suite B algorithms should be used in protocols like IPsec, TLS, S/MIME, SSH, and certificate management.

In July 2015, NSA announced the Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite as the successor to Suite B. CNSA uses stronger algorithms and larger key sizes. As a result, the original Suite B specifications are now only of historical interest; NSA no longer supports Suite B, and the web pages specifying the algorithms are no longer available.
sections.plainLanguage: A government agency said "use these math rules for secrets". Years later they said "actually, use these newer, better rules instead". So the old rulebooks get moved to a library shelf.

sections.title: The Ten RFCs Affected
sections.content:
The ten RFCs reclassified to Historic status are: RFC 4869 (Suite B for IPsec), RFC 5008 (Suite B in S/MIME, later obsoleted by RFC 6318), RFC 5430 (Suite B for TLS, later obsoleted by RFC 6460), RFC 5759 (Suite B Certificate Profile), RFC 6239 (Suite B for SSH), RFC 6318 (Suite B in S/MIME), RFC 6379 (Suite B for IPsec), RFC 6380 (Suite B Profile for IPsec), RFC 6403 (Suite B Profile for Certificate Management), and RFC 6460 (Suite B Profile for TLS).

The first three (4869, 5008, 5430) were already obsoleted by later RFCs; reclassifying them as Historic clarifies that they are no longer current. The remaining seven were published more recently but are now superseded by CNSA Suite specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: All ten old rulebooks are put into the archive. Some had already been replaced by newer versions; the others are being replaced now.

sections.title: Impact and Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that reclassifying these documents to Historic status raises no interoperability or security concerns. The cryptographic algorithms themselves are still defined in other RFCs. For example, if an implementation continues to use the Suite-B-GCM-128 cipher suite name defined in RFC 4869, that is fine because the suite definitions refer to algorithms defined elsewhere.

Other RFCs that reference the Suite B documents (such as RFC 6187, RFC 6605, and RFC 7525) are unaffected in their Standards Track or BCP status. Their content remains valid even though they cite Suite B documents that are now Historic.
sections.plainLanguage: Even though the rulebook is in the archive, the actual game pieces (the math rules) are still defined elsewhere. So old games that use those pieces still work fine.

sections.title: Moving to CNSA Suite
sections.content:
Operators and systems using Suite B are encouraged to transition to CNSA Suite, which uses updated algorithms: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) with larger key sizes, ECDSA with larger curves, and SHA-384 for hashing. The CNSA Suite offers stronger security guarantees for sensitive applications.

The RFC notes that no protocol changes are required for Suite B implementations to become Historic. The transition is administrative: systems can continue to support Suite B where needed for legacy compatibility, but new implementations should follow CNSA Suite recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rulebook (CNSA) is stronger and better, so new games should follow it. Old games can still use the old rules, but they should upgrade when they get a chance.
